paragraphs.text: This tea was grown in [Nantou](nantou:where-it-is), the county in the middle of Taiwan and the only one that does not touch the sea. It is the island's [biggest tea county](nantou:why-people-value-it), with more than half of its plantings, and within its borders the land climbs from low hills to cold mountain gardens. The record names the county and no township, and here it is the township that tells a roasted tea from a light [high mountain](nantou:altitude-bands) one.

The leaf is from 2024, so it is two years old. Taiwan has a tradition of keeping oolong for years as [lao cha](taiwan-oolong:ageing), old tea. No standard says when an oolong becomes old, but those who give a figure put it between ten and thirty years, so this is a young tea.

It is a rolled [oolong](oolong:definition), the partly oxidised tea that stands between green tea and red tea. Leaf rolled into balls is the common shape of [Taiwan oolong](taiwan-oolong:definition), whose plants and craft came over from Fujian.

brewing.text: Ball-rolled Taiwan oolong takes hot water, about 90 to 100°C, a fairly generous amount of leaf and short steeps; the balls open slowly and give many infusions. Roasted Dong Ding takes water from about 95°C to a full boil. Aged oolong takes very hot water, in a pot that holds its heat, clay above all. Oriental Beauty is the exception and takes cooler water, about 80 to 95°C.

notice.text: In light high mountain tea: a sweet, floral cup, often creamy or buttery, with little bitterness and a long sweet aftertaste. In roasted Dong Ding: caramel, ripe fruit, nuts and a toasted aroma. In Baozhong: floral notes and a clear, bright liquor. In Oriental Beauty: ripe fruit and honey, with little bitterness.
